title: Assessment grids that differ between trials
question: When two trials assess progression on different visit schedules, how much does treating recorded event times as exact bias a transported RMST difference, and do midpoint imputation or an interval-censored model remove it?
design: Unanchored comparison of two single arms with Weibull event times, 32 cells crossing each trial's assessment spacing (0 to 3 months), the event rate and the true difference; naive, midpoint and interval-censored analyses of RMST at 24 months. 1000 replicates per cell.
answer: Treating visit-recorded event times as exact biases a cross-trial RMST difference by half the spacing times the event probability by the horizon, with the sign set by which trial visits less often. A 3-month difference in spacing produced a spurious difference of 1.4 months with no true effect, and removed 1.0 of a true 1.2 months in another scenario. Moving events to the interval midpoint or fitting an interval-censored model reduced the bias below 0.1 month.
findings: Naive bias on the prediction (d_B/2)F_B(tau) - (d_A/2)F_A(tau): slope 1.014 (SE 0.005) over 32 scenarios.
Where the schedules differed by 2 months or more, naive bias was 0.94 to 1.43 months in absolute value; materiality confirmed in all 16 such scenarios.
Midpoint shift: largest bias 0.081 months; interval-censored Weibull: 0.071 months.

The registered control (equal schedules, zero bias) failed in 2 of 8 cells, both where the arms' event probabilities differed; there the bias matched the mechanism's prediction (-0.14 and -0.14 against -0.14 and -0.11).
not_answered: Binary event-by-time endpoints, different maximum follow-up, reconstruction error from digitized curves and visit-window jitter were not simulated. Peer review has not been done.
estimand: Difference in restricted mean survival time at 24 months, B minus A
